• Common name: Dwarf ambulia
  • Other names: Ambulia, Ambulis, Asian marshweed
  • Difficulty: Easy
  • Lighting: Low to high
  • Optimal pH: 5.0–7.0
  • Optimal GH: 1–10
  • Optimal temperature: 20–28°C
  • Substrate: Any
  • Can be grown emersed: Partially
  • Growth rate: Fast
  • Placement in tank: Background
  • Height: 25–50 cm
  • Fertilizers: Low requirements
  • CO2: Needed
  • Propagation: Vegetatively
  • Colour: Green

• Origin: Asia
  • Height: 15 - 30+ cm (average height after two months in the tank)
  • Light demand: low
  • CO2: low

Limnophila sessiliflora was listed as a problematic/invasive weed species in the U.S.A. under Act № 36 of 1983 and in South Africa under the Federal Noxious Weed List of 1999. This makes it illegal to import this species into these countries.

Unless you are completely sure that the plant is safe, for example, it was grown in sterile/laboratory conditions (in vitro) and the in vitro pot is not damaged or opened, quarantine and disinfect it first to avoid the risk of contamination and poisoning. Do not introduce a new plant to your tank right after you bought it.

  • The plant can have parasites, pests like snails, or even predators (dragonfly, damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It may already contain residues of chemicals (pesticides) used to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp, and other invertebrates.

This plant is endemic to Asia. It is documented as a major weed problem in paddy rice fields of India, Sri Lanka, China, northeastern parts of Taiwan, Japan, the Philippines, Indochina, and Malaysia.

It can also be found in tropical to subtropical Africa, Australia, and the Pacific Islands.

Limnophila sessiliflora was first brought to the United States as an aquarium plant. In 1965, it was first documented in Lake Seminole (Florida/Georgia) and has since been found in multiple Florida counties and southwestern Georgia. In Texas, it has been reported in the upper San Marcos River (Hays County), Landa Lake on the Comal River (Comal County), and Sheldon Reservoir (Harris County).
This versatile plant thrives in various aquatic habitats, ranging from stagnant and slow-moving rivers and streams, marshy areas, ditches, ponds, and rice fields to lakes, and damp soils.

Due to its significant size and very fast growth rate, Limnophila sessiliflora is only suited to larger (especially tall) aquariums starting from 80 litres (20 gallons).

Over time, this plant will become so large that you will have no choice but to trim and divide it.

In aquariums, Limnophila sessiliflora is usually used as a classic stem plant, planted along the sides or background due to its larger size.

Under optimal conditions, be ready to trim this plant weekly, since it can grow extremely fast. Do not allow the plant to reach the surface. Start trimming when there are 10–15 cm (4–6 inches) left to the water surface. You can safely shorten it by half.

  • Frequent trimming will gradually make the plant bushier as it can branch out at the cut.
  • Trim the plant in a staggered pattern, ensuring that lower levels of the plant receive light. Otherwise, if light doesn't reach the lower leaves, the plant sheds them and becomes leggy.
  • If the lower part of your plant has become bare, you can cut off a healthy top and plant it separately. The remaining unattractive portion can simply be cut down to the roots and left; the root system will produce new growth.

Planting

It is better to plant stems about 5 cm (2 inches) apart and make sure they do not shade other plants.

Plant it deep enough in the substrate to keep it from floating up; there is no special method or trick involved. If you plant after trimming and it keeps floating, you can leave it floating until its root system develops and it is ready to be planted in the substrate. Although it can continue to grow and develop roots when floating, it is not recommended to leave it like that for the long term.

Propagation

  • By seeds. Its flowers produce viable seeds. According to a study, each flower can produce up to 150 seeds, with a germination rate of up to 96%.
  • Vegetative (cuttings). In aquariums, this is the main method of propagation. Simply cut off the stems and plant them, making sure the cutting is at least 5–7 cm (2–3 inches) long. In a week, the new plant will already have a root system.

Common problems

  • Fragile. The leaf blades are sensitive to mechanical damage (though not as much as Hornwort). Solution: handle them with care during maintenance.
  • Brown leaves. The lower leaves lose their green colour and become slightly brownish when the plant grows too big. Solution: check your lighting and nutrition. You can also trim the top and replant it while completely removing the lower part.
  • Leggy. When the stem reaches the water surface, the plant may shed leaves at the lower part. Solution: trim it or place it behind driftwood or rocks to hide the bare stem.
  • Fast growth/overgrowth. It can shade its neighbours. Under high lighting, fertilization and CO2 it can grow very fast and will require a lot of clipping. Solution: regular stem trimming to prevent it from overtaking the whole tank.
  • Relocation. This plant does not like to be moved. If you plan to relocate or remove it, be very cautious and do not pull it out. Solution: cut it down to the roots or proceed with care.

Temperature: Limnophila sessiliflora does best in warm tropical temperatures of 20–28°C (68–82°F). It can also tolerate cold water down to 15°C (60°F); it will just start growing slowly.

pH: Practically all articles dedicated to this plant indicate that it can grow within a pH range of 6 to 8. This is indeed true, as the plant is highly resilient and not demanding of conditions. However, according to research, the optimal pH range is 5 to 7, so slightly acidic water is preferable.

Hardness: It can grow in soft and hard water, GH 1–20. However, in the author's experience, it grows better and faster in soft to moderately hard water (GH 1–10).

Flow: It can tolerate moderate water movement, but avoid strong currents. It does not like them.

Lighting: This plant will generally grow under any lighting conditions, making it suitable even for low-tech tanks. However, under moderate to high lighting, its growth accelerates significantly. Maintain a standard photoperiod of 10–12 hours daily.

There is an opinion that the plant keeps a more lush quality under low light, whereas under strong light it tends to stretch out and become "leggy". The author does not agree: it has been observed multiple times that under strong lighting the distance between nodes decreases significantly, whereas under low lighting it increases.

A sure sign that the plant lacks light is when its top leaves droop downward. If the leaves are upright and cover the stem, the plant is receiving sufficient light. This issue is also directly related to the plant's nutrition and trimming. An interesting feature of this plant is that it slightly folds its leaves at night and reopens them in the morning.

Substrate: Limnophila sessiliflora obtains most of its nutrients from the water column, so sand and even gravel substrates are often recommended. This is true to some degree. It is possible to grow this plant even in inert substrates. However, if you plant it in nutrient-rich substrates you will see how strong its root system can be, and you will see changes in its appearance as well.

CO2: Although CO2 addition promotes growth significantly, using a pressurized CO2 system is not mandatory; it is optional.

Important: It is crucial to maintain a proper balance of CO2 and nutrients for high-light plants. Using intense lighting without CO2 injection and/or fertilization is not recommended, as it can lead to significant algae issues.

Fertilization: The plant needs moderate to high nutrient levels, so regular dosing of liquid plant fertilizers (2–3 times a week) is required.

If you keep shrimp in the tank with this plant, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (many fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Description

  • Growth habit. A perennial erect aquatic plant.
  • Growth form. It grows with submersed and emersed parts. The part growing above water is typically quite short, usually reaching 10–15 cm (4–6 inches).
  • Size. In aquariums, size is essentially limited by the aquarium itself, which is why it is often stated to grow up to 50 cm (20 inches) high and 2.5–5 cm (1–2 inches) wide. In its natural environment, the stems may reach up to 3.7 m (12 feet) in length, growing from the bottom to the surface.
  • Stem. The submerged stem is smooth, about 2–3 mm in diameter. The short emersed part of the stem is erect and covered with fine hairs.
  • Leaves. Submersed and emergent leaves are distinctly different. Emersed leaves are lanceolate and dark green, with torn, uneven, jagged or serrated edges, arranged in 5–8 whorls and about 10–20 mm long. Submerged leaves are finely divided and feathery, about 2.5 cm long, arranged in whorls of 6 or more leaves around the stem; they can be oval, elongated or lance-shaped, generally 10–40 mm long.
  • Flower. Small purplish-blue, blue-violet or pink stalkless axillary flowers, solitary and located on the uppermost part of the stems above the water. In nature, flowering usually continues from July to September (in Texas, through November). Seeds are brown to dark brown and conic to cylindric.
  • Roots. A fairly strong root mass of numerous thin, white roots; it can also produce roots at each stem node.
  • Colour. Green.

Limnophila sessiliflora var. Orange stands out from its typical green counterparts with its orange hue.

Etymology

The genus name "Limnophila" is derived from the Greek words "limne" meaning "marsh or pond" and "philo" meaning "loving", indicating its affinity for aquatic habitats. The species name "sessiliflora" comes from the Latin words "sessilis" meaning "sitting or attached" and "flora" meaning "flower", referring to flowers attached directly to the stem without stalks.

Taxonomy

In 1826, Karl Ludwig von Blume (1796–1862), the German-Dutch botanist, mentioned this species as Limnophila sessiflora. In 1831, G. Bentham corrected the spelling from sessiflora to sessiliflora, and later works have generally accepted the corrected epithet.

  • Kingdom: Plantae
  • Clade: Tracheophytes (vascular plants)
  • Clade: Angiosperms (flowering plants)
  • Clade: Eudicots
  • Order: Lamiales
  • Family: Plantaginaceae
  • Genus: Limnophila
  • Species: Limnophila sessiliflora

Benefits

  • Versatility: It can grow emersed and submersed, in low-tech and high-tech tanks.
  • Removal of excess nutrients: As an extremely fast-growing plant, it absorbs nitrates in large amounts, and absorbs and utilizes harmful substances from animal waste, decayed plant matter and tap water, such as heavy metals, ammonia and nitrites.
  • Reduces algal bloom: The plant is greedy for nutrients, so it outcompetes algae.
  • Hiding place for fish, fry and shrimp: It serves as cover and a hiding place for invertebrates and small fish.
  • Foraging place: It provides biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Oxygenation: Thanks to its serrated leaf surface, it cleans the water of turbidity and oxygenates it.

Conclusion

Limnophila sessiliflora is a fast-growing and versatile plant. It quickly adapts to almost any conditions and absorbs nitrates like a sponge. It can be a great addition to any low-tech or high-tech tank. At the same time, many of these advantages can become a burden over time because the plant requires a lot of trimming and, without proper control, will overshadow everything it can.

In Asian countries, Limnophila sessiliflora is also used as a flavourful spice for fish dishes.

Limnophila sessiliflora is a pretty and undemanding plant from South-East Asia. A great alternative to Cabomba, which doesn't require a lot of light. Stems grow fast up to 40 cm tall and become 3-4 cm wide. The plant often grows leggy in poor light, but this can be counteracted to some extent by stimulating growth with CO2 addition. Most beautiful when planted in groups. In good growing conditions it sends out runners and spreads across the bottom. Limnophila sessiliflora used to be called "Ambulia".
